analysis.one_liner: Expands Social Security benefits for widows, divorced spouses, and students, funded by a payroll surtax on high earners.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or vote; it died in the Senate Finance Committee with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would raise Social Security benefits for widows and widowers, cut the years of marriage a divorced spouse needs to qualify from ten to five, and extend child benefits to age 23 for full-time students, including college students. It would pay for this with a new surtax on income above $400,000: 4% on self-employment income, and 2% each on employees and employers. The bill never received a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor.
analysis.who_benefits: Widows and widowers in two-income households would get a larger survivor benefit — the greater of the deceased spouse's full benefit or 75% of the couple's combined benefits. Divorced spouses would qualify after 5 years of marriage instead of 10, with benefits prorated for shorter marriages. Children of disabled or deceased beneficiaries could keep receiving benefits through age 23 while full-time students, including at college. The new benefits would be financed by a 4% surtax on self-employment income above $400,000 and 2% each on employee wages and employer payrolls above that threshold, with the threshold rising with average wages.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Widows, divorced spouses, and student children

how_it_helps.text: Cuts the marriage-duration requirement for divorced-spouse benefits from 10 years to 5, with benefits phasing in at 10 percentage points per year for marriages between 5 and 10 years.

Raises widow's and widower's benefits to the greater of the deceased spouse's full primary insurance amount or 75% of the sum of both spouses' benefits — a significant increase for widowed people in two-earner couples, who currently lose the lower benefit entirely.

Extends child's insurance benefits from age 19 to age 23 for full-time students, and redefines eligibility to cover any educational institution under the Higher Education Act — so a child of a deceased or disabled worker could keep benefits through college.

Pays for the expansions with a surtax applying only to income above $400,000 (indexed to wage growth): 4% on self-employment income, and 2% each withheld from employees and paid by employers, directed into the Social Security trust funds.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals with income above $400,000 and their employers. Self-employed people pay a 4% surtax on income above the threshold; employees pay 2% of wages above it, and their employers pay a matching 2% excise tax. The $400,000 threshold rises with the national average wage. The bill also credits high earners with a small benefit increase (2% of earnings counted up to $500,000), returning a slice of the new revenue to top earners once they retire.

drawbacks.text: The new surtax raises the cost of high-wage employment: employers would owe 2% on every dollar of pay above $400,000, and the self-employed would owe the full 4%, which opponents of any payroll increase would call a tax hike on high earners and the businesses that pay them the most.

Section 5 folds high earners' earnings above the normal cap (up to $500,000, indexed) into the benefit formula at 2%, so some of the new tax money is immediately returned as higher benefits to the very top of the income distribution — a deliberate sweetener, but one that dilutes the bill's progressivity.

No fiscal or actuarial scoring appears in the record — the Congressional Budget Office and Social Security actuaries never analyzed the bill, so the true cost, the effect on trust-fund solvency, and the size of each expansion were never verified.

Extending child benefits to 23 and easing the divorced-spouse rules would increase program outlays for decades, and without an actuarial estimate there is no way to confirm the surtax fully covers them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is real and targeted at genuinely vulnerable groups — recently divorced older women, widowed spouses in two-earner households, and college-age children of deceased or disabled workers — and the funding is progressive, falling only on income above $400,000. The main honest objections are that the bill was never scored, so no one knows whether the surtax fully covers the expansions or how employers would respond to the 2% tax on very high pay, and that Section 5 hands a small benefit boost back to high earners, trimming the bill's redistribution. A well-designed bill would have gotten an actuarial estimate before moving.

outcome.mechanism: Murray introduced the bill and it was referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which never held a hearing or vote on it before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Patty Murray introduced the Stronger Safety Net Act on March 1, 2018, as a standalone bill with no cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day.
No hearing, markup, vote, or further action of any kind followed; the bill died in committee when the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: People earning above $400,000, and the employers who pay them, are better off because the bill died — they never paid the new surtax. Social Security's benefit rules also remain unchanged, so the trust funds face no new outlays, though widows, divorced spouses, and student children gained nothing either.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners who would have paid the surtax

for.name: Sen. Patty Murray
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it read twice and referred to the Finance Committee; it was her bill alone, with no cosponsors.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance (Chair Orrin Hatch)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after the bill was referred — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving it to die at the end of the 115th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the only support on record was a single Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors, and the Republican-led Finance Committee never acted on the bill.

industries.note: They would pay a new 4% surtax on self-employment income and 2% on employee wages above $400,000, indexed to wage growth. The bill died, so the tax never took effect.
A new 2% excise tax on every dollar of pay above $400,000 would have raised the cost of retaining very highly paid employees. It was never enacted.

By extending child benefits to age 23 for full-time students at any Higher Education Act institution, the bill would have given students of deceased or disabled beneficiaries more money to stay enrolled. The bill never advanced.
